title: What makes a small-business website look good? A practical design critique
description: A practical critique of what makes a small-business website look good: hierarchy, type, contrast, spacing, real photos, consistent components and a clear call to action, with examples from real projects.
summary: Good small-business website design makes the service clear, establishes trust and gives suitable customers an easy next step. Use readable typography, strong hierarchy, real imagery and navigation built around customer tasks. Check the whole journey on mobile, keep motion purposeful and judge the service pages and enquiry handoff as carefully as the homepage.
takeaways: Looking good is mostly hierarchy, type, contrast and spacing, not decoration.
A beautiful site still has to help a visitor finish one clear task.
Ask a designer for one concrete call to action, consistent components and real photos, not a vague promise of a modern look.

sections.title: Look comes first because look sets trust
sections.body:
A visitor encounters the layout, typography and imagery before reading every word. I want those first choices to make the business feel distinctive and the information easy to approach.

That is why I treat appearance as a business decision, not an artistic one. The work on my website design projects starts with the same question every time: what does this page need a stranger to believe, and what should they do next? A deliberate layout can bring the answer and the next step into view together.

sections.title: Good means pretty and easy to use
sections.body:
I judge a business website on visual quality and how well it supports the customer’s task. The site has to look good enough that a visitor feels they have found a capable business. And it has to let that visitor complete a real task without friction: request a repair, explore a property, find a Mass time, see the work.

Either quality on its own wastes the other. A beautiful page still needs a visible enquiry path. A functional page can also use better typography, photography and spacing to express the quality of the business. Design those together, then check whether real visitors understand and use the page.

sections.title: Hierarchy, type and contrast do the heavy lifting
sections.body:
Most of what makes a page look good is invisible when it works. Headings are sized and spaced so the page reads like an outline, with the most important information first. Body text has room to breathe. Link colours and button styles are consistent. None of this is glamorous, and all of it is noticed when it is missing.

Contrast is the quiet foundation. The W3C's accessibility first checks ask for enough difference between text and background that people with reduced contrast sensitivity can read comfortably. Readable contrast gives the composition a clear foundation. The same introductory checks cover descriptive page titles, headings and appropriate text alternatives for images.

sections.title: Real photos beat clever stock
sections.body:
A small business has an advantage no template can fake: it is real. Photos of the actual workshop, the actual team, the actual finished job look better than polished stock photography because visitors can feel the difference. Stock imagery tends to make a competent local business look anonymous.

The photos do not need to be expensive, but they do need to be considered. I have written more about that in photography, video and animation for websites. The short version is that a few honest, well-composed images from the business's own world carry a page further than a hero image of strangers shaking hands.

sections.title: Consistent components, one clear action
sections.body:
A page looks finished when its parts feel like they belong to the same family. Buttons are the same shape and colour everywhere. Cards line up. The footer is not an afterthought. These are small details, and together they signal that the business sweats small details, which is exactly what a customer wants from a repair, a renovation or a stay.

Then the page needs to make up its mind about what happens next. One primary action, styled the same way on every page, beats four competing options. The visitor should never have to wonder whether the yellow button or the text link is the real way to book.

sections.title: Three projects, three different decisions
sections.body:
There is no single good look. What works depends on what the visitor came to do. Here is how the priorities shifted across three very different projects.

How design priorities change with the job the website has to do
ProjectType of siteWhat the page has to doOne design decision that helps
ABC ApplianceLocal serviceMake a repair request and understand what happens nextService information and coverage stated plainly, with one obvious repair-request action
Okanagan TreehouseAccommodationMake a distinctive property feel worth staying forImmersive photography and story first, with a quiet, consistent path to explore the stay
RCCVCommunityHelp people find Mass times, sacraments and parish newsWelcoming, uncluttered layout with generous spacing and a clear reading order

The shared thread is that each site looks considered rather than assembled. The difference is what the consideration was aimed at.

sections.title: Before and after: one headline rewrite
sections.body:
Here is the kind of change that makes a small-business homepage look and feel better, using a service business as the example.

Before:

Welcome to our website. We are a family owned business proudly serving the Okanagan since 2011. We offer a wide range of services to meet your needs, and we are committed to excellence.

After:

Appliance repair across the Okanagan and Shuswap. Tell us what has stopped working and request a visit.

The second version tells a visitor in one breath what is on offer, where it is available and how to request it. That clarity reads as confidence, and confidence reads as good design, even though the visual styling might be identical in both cases.

sections.title: What to ask for when hiring
sections.body:
If you are paying for a new website, ask for specific things rather than a feeling. Ask for a clear page hierarchy with descriptive headings. Ask for text and background colours chosen for readable contrast. Ask for real photos of your business, or at least a plan for getting them. Ask for one primary call to action, styled consistently across the site.

Be cautious of anyone whose answer to everything is a trend, or who treats your content as a placeholder to be figured out later. Cost matters too, and I have written separately about what an Okanagan website tends to cost so the conversation can start from real numbers.

sections.title: A clear way forward
sections.body:
A good-looking website is not a mystery. It is a set of deliberate choices about hierarchy, type, contrast, spacing, imagery and one clear action, made with a specific visitor in mind. When those choices are made well, the site looks good because it works, and it works because it looks like someone cared.

If you would like a set of eyes on your current site, or a plan for a new one, book a free conversation. We can look at what is already working and decide what deserves attention first.

faqs: Does a good-looking website help my Google ranking?

I would not promise a ranking boost from looks alone. What Google has consistently said is that clear, indexable content and the usual sound website fundamentals matter. A well-structured, readable page that visitors stay on and act on tends to be built the same way, so the goals usually support each other.
Do I need professional photos, or will a phone do?

A phone can be enough if the images are honest, well lit and composed with some care. What rarely works is default stock photography, because it makes a real local business look generic. If the budget only stretches to one thing, a handful of genuine photos of your own work is usually the better spend.
How do I know if my current website is the problem?

Try the simple version first: read your homepage out loud and ask whether a stranger would know what you offer and what to do next. Then look at the design basics in this article, such as heading structure, contrast, spacing and whether there is one obvious call to action. If several of those are weak, the design is very likely part of the problem.
How do I judge whether a design will help customers rather than just look impressive?

Follow a customer's real task on a phone: identify the service, decide whether the business fits and make an enquiry. Check whether photography, headings and navigation help that task. Ask the designer to explain the role of each major section and show the supporting service pages, not only the homepage.
How much animation should a small-business website use?

Use motion where it explains the work or adds character without delaying the customer's task. Navigation, contact routes and essential text should remain usable when motion is reduced or scripts fail. Review a real mobile page before approving an animation that looks attractive in a desktop design presentation.
